papers.title: Revisiting RadioGalaxyNET: modern detectors for radio galaxy detection and host identification
papers.abstract: RadioGalaxyNET is the public benchmark for finding extended radio galaxies in EMU pilot-survey images, classifying them and locating their infrared hosts. Its best published results date from 2023: 54.5 box AP (Gal-YOLOv8) and 48.1 host keypoint AP (Gal-DINO). We train three current detectors, D-FINE-seg, YOLO26-pose and RF-DETR, on the same data and score them with the benchmark's own evaluation code, which reproduces the published Gal-DINO numbers exactly. All exceed the published results. D-FINE-seg M reaches 67.1 box AP and 72.4 host AP, 12.6 and 24.3 points above the best published results, and the highest host AP of the detectors we tested; on boxes it is level with YOLO26. Its host lead over YOLO26 comes from host-centered images, which make up most of the benchmark. End to end, D-FINE-seg S is the fastest model at 1.9 ms per image; engine against engine, YOLO26 is faster at the same size. We also report what matters for anyone using the benchmark: its scoring protocol adds 5 to 10 AP, its host labels sit at the image center, its box labels are offset from the image by 1.5 pixels, and its images can be rebuilt from the public survey data, which recovers sky positions and doubles as extra training data. We suggest that future work report host identification F1, as a measure closer to catalog use: D-FINE-seg M 71.8, YOLO26-pose M 70.5, RF-DETR 63.8, Gal-DINO 59.2.

papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

papers.title: Neural-Network Approximators for Low-Thrust Multi-Asteroid Rendezvous Optimization
papers.abstract: Designing low-thrust multi-asteroid rendezvous missions requires the coupled selection of asteroid sequences, encounter epochs, and low-thrust trajectories. Lambert transfers support rapid beam search but do not directly describe thrust-limited transfer capacity or propellant consumption. This paper develops two complementary low-thrust neural approximators. The first directly predicts the continuous maximum admissible initial mass from numerically optimized low-thrust transfers, providing a transfer-capacity estimate for comparison with the current spacecraft mass. The second predicts mass-dependent propellant consumption and propagates spacecraft mass to subsequent legs. With the carefully-designed input features and network structure, the approximators reduce mean absolute errors by 72.2% and 75.5%, respectively, relative to conventional deep neural network baselines. These predictions are incorporated into a Lambert-ranked beam search through resource filtering and recursive mass propagation before final beam selection. The method is evaluated on fixed-visit, maximum-visit, and deployment-collection missions. Across the tested cases, the proposed resource filtering increases the fraction of candidate sequences that yield accepted low-thrust solutions, raises the maximum validated asteroid-visit count by up to 15.4%, and improves the best mission objective by up to 17.8%. These results demonstrate that continuous transfer-capacity and propellant predictions can improve finite-width sequence search.

papers.title: Is the learner or the summary the limit? Auditing machine-learning energy reconstruction for air-shower arrays on KASCADE and GRAPES-3
papers.abstract: Machine-learning energy estimators for cosmic-ray arrays are usually trained on a few fitted shower parameters, not station signals. When their resolution stops improving, standard diagnostics cannot say whether a better model would help or the summary has run out of information. We use a five-step audit that compares trained models with a learner-independent estimate of the lowest error the summary allows (its squared-loss Bayes risk, or floor), tests which inputs add information and flags inputs merely computed from the fit. We apply it to public KASCADE simulations with three hadronic-interaction models (QGSJET-II-04, EPOS-LHC and SIBYLL-2.3d), to 13,848,509 measured KASCADE events and to simulated GRAPES-3 events. Within known energy decades below 10^16 eV, gradient boosting on nine reconstructed features is within 2.2% of the estimated floor under every estimator setting, so more capacity is not expected to gain more than about 2%. The floor is an estimate, accurate to about 1% in a semi-synthetic benchmark with intervals that under-cover, and not a bound on the true Bayes risk. Replacing reconstructed by true particle numbers removes 70 to 72% of the error variance below 10^15 eV and 24 to 26% between 10^16 and 10^17 eV on all three models, yet simulated station signals close about a tenth of that gap. On GRAPES-3, networks given images rendered from the fit do no better than the fit. In measured data, the mean muon size at fixed electron size lies within every model's proton-to-iron bracket and a label-free probe finds the muon channel used as in simulation; neither fixes the energy scale. Energy-labelled results are simulated.

papers.title: Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
papers.abstract: Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.

papers.title: From Surface Lakes to Subsurface Signatures in Antarctica with BIOMASS P-Band TomoSAR
papers.abstract: Spaceborne remote sensing of the cryosphere is fundamental to map ice structure and dynamics. Accurate mass balance estimation requires a better understanding of melt/refreeze processes and firn hydrology, whereas spaceborne optical and Radar sensors are mostly limited to near-surface observations. The BIOMASS P-band Synthetic Aperture Radar, launched by European Space Agency in 2025, provides an unprecedented opportunity to gain a more direct access to englacial processes, thanks to the 70 cm wavelength paired with polarimetry, interferometry and tomography. This paper investigates subsurface beneath a region of historical supraglacial lake activity with BIOMASS tomography, at the Riiser-Larsen Ice Shelf in East Antarctica. The main result is that subsurface scattering appears to be related to historical supraglacial lake recurrence, with structural and depth variations over time. This suggests that recurrent supraglacial lake activity may leave persistent hydrological signatures within the firn. Overall, this study highlights the potential of gaining valuable insights into ice sheet hydrology with P-band.

papers.title: The Simons Observatory: Analysis of methods for polarization calibration of multiple instruments
papers.abstract: Cosmic birefringence, the rotation of the CMB linear polarization plane across the Universe, is a powerful test of parity-violating physics beyond the Standard Model. Static isotropic rotation, however, is limited by an instrument's absolute polarization-angle calibration. We present a method for transferring absolute calibration between Simons Observatory (SO) instruments, validated on map-level simulations of the Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) and Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) with lensed CMB polarization, polarized Galactic foregrounds, correlated instrumental noise, and polarization-angle miscalibration. We develop two pipelines: a joint LAT+SAT likelihood transferring calibration through their overlap, and the Minami-Komatsu foreground-based method, which separates cosmic birefringence from instrumental miscalibration using Galactic dust polarization without an external angle prior. We derive a general variance budget showing that calibration transfer improves sensitivity only when the combined reference and overlap transfer uncertainties remain below the receiving instrument's calibration uncertainty. While transfer does not lower the absolute-angle floor for isotropic $\beta$, it anchors the receiving instrument's multipole range. The relative-angle uncertainty is $\sim 0.1^\circ$ for $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=300$, improving to $\sim 0.04^\circ$ at $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=600$, subject to SAT beam and transfer-function control. Finally, for $\beta=0.3^\circ$, we show how the LAT's $\ell$-range distinguishes scale-independent dark-energy rotation from scale-dependent axion dark-matter models via $C_\ell^{EB}$.

papers.title: Reliability of Fermi/GBM spectral-catalogue parameters for gamma-ray burst population studies
papers.abstract: The Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) spectral catalogue contains measurements affected by model uncertainties, different peak-flux (PFLX) integration times, and changes in catalogue processing. We examine which quantities describe spectral shape and which reflect brightness or measurement conditions. We analysed 3337 of 3378 GRBs with spectral-fit data and identified a catalogue transition at GRB180712358. We compared the two periods using rank-based tests, regressions, and catalogue model-selection rules, and assessed duration classification by repeated cross-validation. PFLX measurements at 64 and nominal 1024 ms were analysed separately; short-long comparisons used fluence (FLNC) measurements only. The transition coincides with changes in catalogue version, fit statistic, and fit fields. In the nominal 1024 ms sample, all ten COMP A-B rank-biserial effects have absolute values below 0.10. In the 64 ms sample, COMP shape parameters are similar, but amplitudes, fluxes, and fluences are higher in the later period. The origin of this difference is unknown. In the earlier period, brighter bursts have smaller parameter errors but larger reported fit statistics and stronger evidence for spectral curvature. The FLNC PLAW index measures broad-band hardness. BAND alpha and Epeak can describe spectral shape when their errors are controlled, but beta is often poorly constrained. Adding PLAW or BAND to COMP provides little additional duration-classification information in matched samples. We interpret the A-B division mainly as a catalogue-processing transition, not population evolution. Fit statistics, errors, metadata, and model labels describe measurement conditions and should not be treated as independent physical variables. Correlated model parameters should not be treated as independent.

papers.title: JAISP: A Joint Rubin-Euclid Foundation Model for Cross-Instrument Source Detection and Astrometry
papers.abstract: Joint pixel-level processing of Rubin and Euclid imaging promises deeper source detection and the cross-survey consistency that precision cosmology requires. We introduce JAISP (Joint AI Survey Processing), a foundation model that learns a single representation of ten-band imaging: Rubin ugrizy and Euclid VIS, Y, J, and H, from the first public releases over $\approx 0.2$ deg$^2$ of the ECDFS deep field. Trained without labels by predicting each band from the other nine, its frozen encoder drives small task-specific networks for source detection and astrometry. The detection network recovers nearly all VIS-selected Euclid Q1 catalog sources on held-out sky, and source injection shows that combining all ten bands extends the point-source detection limit by $\approx 0.3$ mag beyond VIS alone. The astrometry network transfers the sharp VIS localization to the other nine bands, reducing median cross-band positional offsets from $\approx 50$ to $6$--$10$ mas while retaining the full precision of its VIS centroid anchor even for faint sources. Separating this per-source scatter exposes the cross-survey concordance field: a coherent $9$--$10$ mas offset between the two independently Gaia-registered astrometric solutions, dominated by a component common to all bands. Applied without retraining to a second Euclid Deep Field, both networks perform without measurable loss. These gains serve the joint-survey science case: a deeper census recovers faint neighbors whose blending biases weak-lensing shapes and photometric redshifts, and VIS-grade positions in every band supply the common astrometric reference that joint photometry and faint-source proper motions require. A single representation learned once from survey pixels thus serves several measurements across the sky.

papers.title: Correlation Calibration: A Hybrid Calibration Technique for Radio Interferometric Arrays
papers.abstract: Calibrating out per-antenna signal chain effects is an essential step in analyzing radio interferometric data. For drift-scanning arrays, robustly calibrating the data is especially challenging due to the lack of the ability to track a calibration source. Consequently, calibration strategies for drift-scanning arrays are limited by our knowledge of the radio sky at large, as well as the direction-dependent instrument response. In the context of 21 cm cosmology, where small calibration errors can conspire to overwhelm the cosmological signal, it is therefore crucially important to develop calibration strategies that are capable of accurately calibrating the data in the presence of sky or instrument modeling errors. In this paper we present CorrCal, a covariance-based calibration strategy for radio interferometric arrays. CorrCal is a hybrid calibration strategy that leverages the strengths of traditional sky-based calibration and redundant calibration in a computationally efficient framework that is fairly insensitive to modeling errors. We find that calibration errors from CorrCal are unbiased and far below typical thermal noise thresholds across a wide range of modeling error scenarios. We show that CorrCal is computationally efficient: our implementation is capable of evaluating the likelihood and its gradient in less than a second for 1,000-element class arrays using just a single laptop core. Given CorrCal's computational efficiency and robustness to modeling errors, we anticipate that it will serve as a useful tool in the analysis of radio interferometric data from current and next-generation experiments targeting the cosmological 21 cm signal.

papers.title: Equivalence of mapping gravitational wave background anisotropy across bases at equal information content
papers.abstract: Mapping anisotropies in the gravitational-wave background (GWB) requires choosing a basis to represent the sky intensity, such as pixel and spherical harmonic bases. Each introduces a truncation---e.g., a number of pixels or a maximum multipole l_max---often set by a naive counting argument that relate the number of measurable modes to the number of independent cross-correlations, N_pair, in a pulsar timing array (PTA). However, such truncations can lead to reconstruction artifacts, as they do not reflect the true information content of the PTA response. Increasing the value of truncation parameters spans the observable space better but reveals poorly constrained modes, making the inverse problem ill conditioned and requiring regularization. A natural approach is to restrict the reconstruction to a well-measured subspace via principal maps, defined by the dominant eigenmodes of the detector response (or Fisher) matrix. However, these maps are not a fundamental parametrization of the sky but, rather, are derived from an underlying representation---such as a pixelization or a spherical harmonic expansion. While their explicit form depends on basis choice, they can span the \textit{same subspace} when the underlying representation is sufficiently complete. Here, we show that reconstructed anisotropy maps via different bases are equivalent, provided they retain the same information content, i.e., span the same principal subspace. As illustrative cases, we consider a toy model for PTA configuration and several GWB anisotropy shapes: point source, an extended source with deterministic anisotropy, and a statistical isotropic background, along with its summary statistic---the angular power spectrum. Although the reconstructions are equivalent, their computational costs can differ. We conclude with brief comments on the construction of principal maps for ground-based interferometers.

papers.abstract: This paper reviews how Euclid's top-level calibration requirements were translated into a calibration plan, how this plan is implemented and maintained during the survey, and how it performs in the current DR1 release. We show that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements. The construction of spectroscopically complete and pure samples relies on ongoing data acquisition for the Euclid Deep Survey, while point-spread-function modelling and shear calibration are still converging to their stringent accuracy requirements. With all DR1 data reprocessed with the DR1 pipeline configuration, more subtle effects have been detected and characterised, and correction strategies have been developed for DR2. These include improved absolute flux calibration, astrometry, charge-persistence correction, shutter effects, wavelength calibration, and spectrophotometric corrections for water-ice contamination. Finally, synthetic photometric transformations between Euclid and each of Roman, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope, are presented.

papers.abstract: The Euclid mission was designed around the need for thermo-optical and mechanical stability, stray-light suppression, low outgassing, and precise guiding. After three years in space, a wealth of data is available to assess the performance in these areas. We review the L2 halo-orbit design and consumables budget. Solar stray-light gradually increases by 14% per year and is consistent with meteoroid puncturing, but remains low overall. Data loss from high solar activity has declined notably since the maximum of the 25th Solar cycle passed. The thermodynamical response of the optical elements to a thermal step impulse follows sigmoidal growth curves, entering the asymptotic equilibration regime after 21--46 hours. Water-ice contamination has affected data from both instruments and requires continued monitoring; we review detection and decontamination methods, and Euclid's contamination history. High-precision measurements of the zodiacal background reveal, at eight sigma significance, the subtle modulation caused by the changing perspective on the dust distribution due to the L2 halo-orbit libration. These data also show that conservative pre-launch estimates overestimated the out-of-field stray-light by factors of 4 (H band) to 27 (I band). Telemetry data demonstrate excellent guiding, and enable highly significant detections of solar radiation pressure and of thermal-emission recoil from Euclid's unilluminated dark sides. Lastly, we present a list of 34 meteoroid impacts, discuss their mechanical and optical signatures, and derive a minimum detectable impactor mass of 5e-7 g.

papers.title: On the Sensitivity of Fermi-LAT Maximum Likelihood Stacking
papers.abstract: Stacking sub-threshold gamma-ray sources has become common practice for understanding high-energy emission processes at the population level. In this procedure, one co-adds log-likelihood ratios, called TS values (TS = 2ln$(L_1/L_0)$), for a source class of interest. It is best practice to compare the population of sub-threshold targets against a population of control field test sources (CFs) selected to represent the unmodeled \gray\ background. Determining the significance of a TS measurement stack has typically been difficult. In this work, we find the necessary cumulative TS value ($\Sigma$TS) of a sub-threshold population of $N$ targets to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation from a like-sized population of CFs. We find that the $\Delta (\Sigma$TS) needed to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation is $\sim 70$. In taking this measurement, we characterize the source distribution corresponding to the measured $\Sigma$TS for a significantly detected stack and even predict new individual source detections in larger stacks.

papers.title: The JWST Resolved Stellar Populations Early Release Science Program. X. Cross-Observatory Proper Motion Measurements with HST and JWST
papers.abstract: We present the first absolute systemic proper motion (PM) of a galaxy measured by combining Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and JWST imaging. The PM of WLM, an isolated dwarf galaxy at $\sim$1 Mpc, is measured against background galaxies with Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) F814W imaging from 2015 and 2024 and NIRCam imaging from 2022 and 2024. The two ACS epochs give a systemic PM of $(\mu_{\alpha}^*, \mu_{\delta}) = (+0.087 \pm 0.019, -0.079 \pm 0.017)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 145 galaxies over 8.93 years, which agrees with previous Gaia-based PMs to within 0.4$\sigma$ and is the most precise PM of WLM. For the HST-to-JWST PMs, we fit each NIRCam detector separately, match the point-spread functions with empirically derived convolution kernels, and correct biases with injected galaxies. With an F090W second epoch, the PM is $(+0.081 \pm 0.045, -0.113 \pm 0.046)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 43 galaxies over 7.02 years, which, like the F150W PM, agrees with HST-to-HST over the same area to within 1$\sigma$, while F200W differs by $\sim$2$\sigma$. The long-wavelength F250M and F430M PMs are consistent to within 1$\sigma$, though less precise. Fewer galaxies can be used at wavelengths farther from F814W. A cross-observatory systematic of $\sim$0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ cannot be ruled out over 7 years. At equal baselines, an F090W second epoch is at least as precise as our second ACS epoch over the same area. We recommend the NIRCam filter closest in wavelength to the first-epoch filter, though the long-wavelength filters show promise for closer targets or longer baselines.

papers.title: Constraining Planet Nine with Pulsar Timing: Orbit Determination Method from the Acceleration, Jerk, and Snap of the Solar System Barycenter
papers.abstract: Planet Nine is hypothesized to exist in the outer solar system in order to explain the physical orbital clustering of several trans-Neptunian objects. A Planet Nine would systematically change the location of the solar system barycenter (SSB). Therefore, the precise timing properties of millisecond radio pulsars would measure the acceleration, jerk, and snap of the currently-perceived SSB under the gravitational influence of a Planet Nine. We present a method on how to use pulsar spin frequency derivatives and binary pulsar orbital period derivatives to constrain the Planet Nine parameter space. We find that searches for unidentified massive objects in the solar system require at least cubic and quartic variations in the pulse times of arrival (corresponding to jerk and snap, respectively) in order to uniquely constrain an orbit. Otherwise, additional assumptions are required to fully constrain the mass and orbital parameters of the object. We use our method to weigh the ice giants Uranus and Neptune and obtain results consistent with the literature. This method could be used to weigh a Planet Nine after a putative optical detection. Future work will use updated pulsar timing datasets that benefit from longer observational baselines and advances in statistical modeling and noise characterization.

papers.title: DIPS-OjOS I: Project Design and Science Validation
papers.abstract: Automated pipelines and machine-learning algorithms are efficient at detecting standard planetary transits, but can miss subtle, non-periodic morphological anomalies. We present the pilot phase of DIPS-OjOS (Detecting Irregular Photometric Signals - Oj\'imetrO Survey), a professional-amateur collaboration designed to develop and validate a scalable workflow for identifying irregular photometric signals in exoplanet transit light curves through trained visual inspection. The project targets starspot-crossing events, stellar flares, circumplanetary structures, exomoon-like signatures, and transit-duration or timing anomalies overlooked by automated searches. We built the infrastructure required for a controlled visual-inspection experiment: simulated control light curves, preparation and detrending of real short-cadence Kepler data, a transit-modeling pipeline that computes an optimized average transit profile for each light curve, and a web-based classification platform. The real sample was deliberately restricted to 51 well-characterized Kepler systems. Collaborators inspected 917 transit events: 555 real transits and 362 simulated controls. The simulated sample quantified observer performance and calibrated a weighted consensus scheme; collaborators recovered injected signals with an average efficiency of 87.6%, while the null-case false-positive rate was 15.3%. After expert validation, we retained 88 viable candidate anomalies from the real sample, including 26 starspot-crossing event candidates across eight targets, seven stellar flares, 31 systematic transit-duration deviations motivating refined orbital parameters in four systems, and a mutual transit event in Kepler-89. Recovering candidate signals in this well-studied sample validates the sensitivity of DIPS-OjOS and establishes the basis for future applications to Kepler, TESS, PLATO, and ground-based datasets.

papers.title: Validating Gaia DR3 Astrometric Accelerations with Close Visual Binaries
papers.abstract: We validate a subset of the astrometric accelerations reported in Gaia DR3 non-single-star solutions by their consistency with the gravitational pull of known, resolved companions. Cross-matching 338,215 DR3 acceleration solutions against the Washington Double Star (WDS) catalog of visual binaries yields 2,466 unique pairs within 2". For each pair we compare the measured acceleration with alpha_max, the Newtonian bound on the acceleration the companion can impart on the Gaia-tracked photocenter. For 98.1% of the pairs the measured acceleration exceeds this bound by more than a factor of 10, so the cataloged companion cannot be responsible and the perturber must be a closer, unresolved one. The remaining 45 plausible wide binaries are close pairs at the WDS resolution limit. We fit orbits with an updated orvara, extended to accept the DR3 acceleration and jerk coefficients as direct constraints and released with htof as part of this work. The fits converge for 16 of the 45 and one boundary case, the rest having too few resolved measures or a perturber other than the cataloged pair, and 13 of the 17 carry enough data to test the coefficients. Eleven of the 13 statistically accommodate the reported accelerations, for seven- and nine-parameter solutions alike, and the dynamical companion masses agree with the photometric estimates where the photocenter conversion is well determined. Independently of the fits, 33 of the 43 plausible systems with a usable position angle (77%) have the acceleration directed within 45 degrees of the primary-companion axis, against 50% for a control sample: DR3's measured accelerations point in the directions of the cataloged companions.

papers.title: Probabilistic Inversion of Strong Gravitational Lenses with Flow Matching Priors
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing reveals important information about the universe, but reconstructing the source image and lens properties requires solving an ill-posed inverse imaging problem. Generative image models serve as powerful data-driven priors in Bayesian inverse problems. Diffusion models have been used widely, but they are computationally costly. Flow matching has emerged as a promising alternative to diffusion models, with easier training, efficient sampling, and better-quality data generation. In this work, we present Blind-FlowSGS, a principled blind posterior sampling method using flow matching priors, enabling efficient posterior sampling for non-blind and blind inversion of strong gravitational lenses. On simulated Euclid data, we demonstrate our method's improvement over diffusion-based methods in both efficacy and efficiency. Our method shows promising capabilities to accurately process strong lensing data from modern sky surveys at scale. Our code and data are available on our project page.

papers.title: Analysis of the Cosmos 2612 - ICEYE-X36 rendezvous and proximity operation from public orbital element data
papers.abstract: We analyse the October 2026 close approach between Cosmos 2612 (NORAD 68762) and the commercial radar satellite ICEYE-X36 (NORAD 59103), both in sun-synchronous low Earth orbit, to determine whether it was a rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO) or the result of natural orbital evolution. The public general perturbations (GP) element history from April to October 2026 was propagated with SGP4, and the prediction error was measured empirically for each object. The null hypothesis of natural evolution, tested with manoeuvre-free propagations, is rejected for all 18 parameter combinations: the encounter required manoeuvres by Cosmos 2612, whereas those of ICEYE-X36 are not needed to reproduce it. Closest approach occurred on 18 October at 06:33 UTC, below 0.79 km (95th percentile), with a local relative velocity of about 0.08 m/s and 41.4 h continuously within 5 km. It was the final stage of a sequence that began in May with a plane match, followed by a phasing drift, the approach and a manoeuvred retreat, with a minimum cumulative $\Delta v$ of 174-180 m/s. The data cannot resolve the minimum distance below their accuracy, nor establish whether the operation was cooperative or its purpose.

papers.title: py4radiation: a framework for generating heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom radiation fields for astrophysical simulations
papers.abstract: Modelling multiphase gas in and around galaxies is key to understanding the baryon cycle in galaxy evolution. Modern simulation codes rely on heating/cooling functions and ion fractions to capture the thermodynamics and chemistry of such gases, but coupling all physical factors remains challenging. We present a new Python-based, parallelised package that acts as an integration framework, connecting well-established astrophysical codes and models to produce self-consistent heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom ionising UV/X-ray backgrounds. The package returns multi-dimensional tables that can be readily coupled to hydrodynamic and post-processing codes to study radiative processes and extract observables, as we demonstrate with static cloud simulations. Our simulation suite studies the thermodynamic history of a static circumgalactic cloud with smoothed edges subjected to meta-galactic and starburst heating. We find that the clouds experience damped pulsations regulated by strong cooling-driven inflows and heating-driven outflows that constantly overshoot pressure equilibrium. Meta-galactic heating is weak and produces a confined and dense cloud, while starburst heating is strong and sustains large clouds only a little smaller than those obtained with the standard $10^4\,\rm K$ cooling floor. Starburst radiative heating acts as a damping agent, thereby reducing mixing. py4radiation comes with extensive documentation and a sample catalogue of heating/cooling functions and ion tables for a selected set of input meta-galactic and starburst spectral energy distributions. The code is publicly available and can be easily expanded.

papers.title: Predicting the Orbital Retention of Habitable-Zone Planets Following Stellar Flybys Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Stellar flybys can significantly alter the orbital configurations of planetary systems, potentially displacing planets initially located within the habitable zone (HZ) of their host stars. In this study, we investigate the dynamical effects of stellar encounters on HZ planets using a large suite of three-body N-body simulations. We examine how the properties of the host star, passing star, planetary orbit, and encounter geometry influence the final orbital configuration. A planet is considered to retain an HZ orbit only if it remains bound to its original host and its entire final orbital range, from periastron to apastron, lies within the HZ boundaries. Based on the simulation results, we develop an XGBoost classifier to predict the final HZ status of planets following stellar encounters. The model achieves an accuracy of 0.90, an ROC-AUC of 0.97, and a PR-AUC of 0.97 on the test set. Feature importance analysis identifies the encounter-impulse parameter as the dominant predictor of the outcome. The classifier provides a computational speedup of approximately 74 compared with direct N-body simulations. We further evaluate the model using an independent dataset representing a globular-cluster environment, where approximately 20 per cent of planets retain HZ orbits. Despite the naturally imbalanced class distribution, the model achieves an accuracy of 0.87, an ROC-AUC of 0.92, and a PR-AUC of 0.77. These results demonstrate the potential of machine learning for efficiently predicting the dynamical retention of HZ planets following stellar encounters and for investigating their outcomes in dense stellar environments.

papers.title: Performance of attention-based deep-learning models in Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor measurements
papers.abstract: A systematic performance evaluation of attention-based deep-learning models for wavefront reconstruction in Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (SHWFS) systems is presented. While deep learning has been extensively applied to pyramid and focal-plane wavefront sensing, its application to standard SHWFS configurations remains relatively underexplored. A simulation dataset consisting of 3.5 million open-loop uncorrelated turbulent phase and image pairs modeled after the Subaru Telescope pupil was generated. The dataset spans four pupil-sampling cases (8$\times$8, 16$\times$16, 20$\times$20, and 32$\times$32 subapertures) under realistic conditions. A custom Vision Transformer (ViT) which incorporates features such as rotary positional embeddings, register tokens, and a cross-attention decoder, is benchmarked against a fully convolutional U-Net and a classical Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) linear reconstructor. The results show that the ViT architecture yields the lowest overall residual phase variance across all tested subaperture configurations, demonstrating a robust capability to model global spatial correlations and spot-to-spot cross-coupling across the pupil. While the U-Net performs competitively by capturing localized features, it exhibits $\sim1.5$ times more residual variance per mode than the ViT, which is relatively significant in high-order modes. This study represents a key step toward implementing attention-based models for high-order wavefront sensing and telemetry-assisted data reduction in next-generation instrument suites like ULTIMATE-Subaru.

papers.title: Stellar Temporal Intensity Interferometry with Adaptive Optics at the Palomar Observatory
papers.abstract: Spatial intensity interferometry has seen a major resurgence in astronomy due to its immunity to atmospheric phase turbulence, but its temporal counterpart - a cornerstone of quantum optics - has remained largely unexplored for astronomical sources. Here, we demonstrate that high-visibility temporal photon bunching signatures from stellar sources are now accessible by combining ultra-narrowband spectral filtering with high-speed single-photon counting detectors. Leveraging the adaptive optics architecture at the Palomar Observatory, we report the first observation of resolved stellar temporal photon bunching, with a peak of $g^{(2)}(\tau=0) = 1.3 \pm 0.1$, from the red supergiant $\alpha$ Her. This advance establishes stellar temporal intensity interferometry as a viable observational modality, bridging quantum optics with high-resolution stellar astrophysics.

papers.title: Luminosity function of millisecond pulsars in globular clusters from their gamma-ray emission
papers.abstract: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are widely believed to be responsible for the gamma-ray emission of globular clusters (GCs), yet the underlying MSP gamma-ray luminosity function remains uncertain. Existing GC-based determinations of the latter often rely on external prescriptions for the number of MSPs in each cluster. In this work, we constrain the MSP gamma-ray luminosity function in Milky-Way GCs directly from gamma-ray spectral energy distributions (SEDs), establishing an inference strategy that remains computationally viable for joint analyses of large GC samples. We construct a forward model in which each GC hosts a population of MSPs whose luminosities are drawn from a universal log-normal luminosity function. Synthetic GC SEDs are generated by summing individual MSP spectra, and we infer posterior distributions using first a likelihood-based nested sampling method and then a simulation-based inference (SBI) approach. We show how the likelihood-based method becomes rapidly impractical as the number of jointly modelled clusters (and cluster-specific latent parameters) increases, whereas the SBI approach scales mildly with sample size and reproduces the likelihood-based posteriors in regimes where direct sampling is feasible. We then apply the SBI pipeline to Fermi-LAT SEDs from the 4FGL-DR4 catalog for a sample of 36 GC-associated sources, augmented by dedicated phase-resolved ON/OFF SEDs for two clusters hosting individually detected MSPs. For the real data sample, we obtain informative constraints on the luminosity-function parameters consistent with previous analyses that constrain the cluster-specific MSP counts via complementary multi-wavelength information.

papers.title: Cross-calibration of Hera/HyperScout-H with MRO/CRISM and MEx/OMEGA based on Mars observations
papers.abstract: On March 12, 2025, Hera, the European Space Agency's planetary defense mission, performed a Mars flyby en route to the asteroid system (65803) Didymos-Dimorphos. During this event, HyperScout-H (HS-H), the spacecraft's hyperspectral imager, acquired five high spatial resolution images over the southern hemisphere of Mars. These observations provide an opportunity for systematic cross-calibration of HS-H with two established Mars orbital instruments, Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Murchie et al., 2007), and Observatoire pour la Min\'eralogie, l'Eau, les Glaces et l'Activit\'e (OMEGA) on board Mars Express (Bibring et al., 2004). This study evaluates the performance, reliability, and readiness of HS-H for the forthcoming asteroid observation phase by comparing it with CRISM and OMEGA data. We selected 21 surface regions spanning diverse terrain types from three HS-H images in which the Martian surface fills the entire field of view. These images were corrected, calibrated, and co-registered to associate each pixel with latitude and longitude. The relative inter-channel correction factors are close to unity for bands 3-25 (0.688-0.952 {\mu}m), with standard deviations of 0.52% for OMEGA and 0.62% for CRISM, indicating good agreement in spectral shape. Bands 1 and 2 show a systematic mismatch of 4.7% and 3.6%. The absolute flux correction factors reveal offsets of 8% relative to OMEGA and approximately 0.7% relative to CRISM, with mean inter-image standard deviations below 2%. These results confirm the radiometric stability of HS-H and establish a calibration framework for future Didymos-Dimorphos observations.

papers.title: Characterization of solar background signatures in IXPE gas pixel detectors through laboratory measurements
papers.abstract: We present a laboratory to in-flight comparison of the IXPE background signatures, using the spare Detector Unit (DU), identical to the three flight units, exposed to a Co-60 radioactive source, historically adopted as a proxy for solar-induced X-ray background. Co-60 emits 1.17 MeV and 1.33 MeV photons which undergo Compton scattering in the DU structures, producing a degraded spectrum extending down to the keV range after ADC counts to keV conversion via Fe-55 (charging measurement) calibration. The source was placed on the top and side of the DU; event tracks were reconstructed to extract spectral and morphological observables (track size, energy fraction in the track's main cluster, number of pixel triggered per event). Laboratory spectra and parameter distributions are compared with IXPE in-flight in-eclipse (Earth occultating the sun) and in-sun backgrounds from two observations (NGC 2110, RCW 86). We discuss how the in-flight and on-ground spectral and modulation properties of the background compare to each other.

papers.title: A Log-Normal Timing Likelihood for Direction Reconstruction of Ultra-High-Energy Gamma-Ray Air Showers
papers.abstract: Ultra-high-energy $\gamma$-ray observations provide a direct probe of Galactic PeVatrons. Extending measurements to multi-PeV energies requires characterizing extensive air showers over large lateral distances, where the arrival-time distribution of secondary particles becomes broad and strongly asymmetric. Conventional direction reconstruction methods approximate the shower front as a deterministic surface and minimize a $\chi^2$ function of timing residuals. Because this implicitly assumes symmetric Gaussian errors, far-axis timing information is poorly utilized. \textsc{CORSIKA} simulations show that the arrival-time distribution of $\gamma$-induced secondary particles in the shower plane at a given lateral distance is positively skewed and closely follows a log-normal function. Using this property, we develop a likelihood-based direction reconstruction method that directly models the empirical arrival-time distribution and its radial dependence while accounting for multiple particles triggering the same detector unit. Applied to simulated $\gamma$-induced air showers, the log-normal likelihood consistently improves angular resolution compared with conical and parabolic wavefront fits, with the largest relative gains for high-energy events spanning wide lateral extents. We also show that independent readout of individual detector units yields better angular resolution than merging their signals into a single station-level measurement.

papers.title: Reconstructing the depth of first interaction in extensive air showers from fluorescence detector profiles with a physics-motivated neural network
papers.abstract: We present a physics-motivated neural network that reconstructs, event by event, the depth of the first interaction of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays from longitudinal profiles measured by fluorescence detectors. The network couples a convolutional encoder to a decoder that implements the Gaisser-Hillas function and predicts quantiles of the target, providing a per-event uncertainty estimate. It is trained and evaluated on four million proton- and iron-induced showers between $10^{18}$ and $10^{20}$ eV, simulated with the hadronic interaction models EPOS LHC-R and Sibyll 2.3d and processed by an end-to-end simulation of the fluorescence detector response. Despite detector effects, the reconstruction retains useful information for protons, achieving a mean absolute error of about 21 g$\,$cm$^{-2}$ for primary energies around $10^{19}$ eV, whereas for iron most of the information is lost. The reconstructed distributions preserve the exponential shape of the true ones, so the proton-air interaction length can be recovered from their tail with a model-related systematic uncertainty of approximately 4%. This value is limited mainly by the choice of the hadronic interaction model and is nearly insensitive to iron contamination. These results show that the depth of the first interaction can be reconstructed under realistic detection conditions, offering a complementary route to measurements of the proton-air cross section and mass-composition studies.

papers.title: Geneva seven-colour synthetic photometry from Gaia DR3 spectrophotometry
papers.abstract: The well-established calibrations of astrophysical parameters derived from classical photometric systems (e.g. those of Johnson, Stromgren-Crawford, and Vilnius) are rarely applied at present. Instead, spectral energy distribution fitting techniques and the very broad Gaia photometric system are typically employed. However, these approaches have proven highly inaccurate for upper main-sequence stars. In this work, the Geneva seven-colour photometric system was synthesised from flux-calibrated low-resolution Gaia spectrophotometry (BP/RP spectra). The available ground-based observations have made it the most homogeneous dataset, offering a number of astrophysical calibrations and applications. The GaiaXPy Tool was used to synthesise the seven filters. The original Geneva U had to be exchanged with the SDSS u because it is found to be significantly blueward of the cut-off of the BP/RP spectra. The ground-based observations were used to correct for offsets and the known temperature dependence of the effective temperature in the ultraviolet region of the BP/RP spectra. The test using well-known effective temperature and metallicity calibrations on the synthetic photometry (with 21 080 stars) demonstrated the high accuracy of this approach. Further checks for possible correlations between the projected rotational velocity and binarity yielded negative results. As a direct application, the metallicity of 630 open clusters (and, thus, the radial Galactic metallicity gradient) was determined. Finally, we compiled a catalogue of 25 881 397 objects. This work demonstrates that alternatives exist to the widely used three-band Gaia photometric system. The Geneva seven-colour approach can help calibrate and analyse astrophysical parameters, especially those of upper main-sequence stars.
